I was unable to fetch every planned source due to tool limits, but I gathered substantial material from Enduring Word (Guzik), Gill’s Exposition, Matthew Henry, Precept Austin, and a relevant John Piper (Desiring God) sermon. I could not retrieve Ellicott, Pulpit, NET Bible notes, or denomination-specific pages (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Pentecostal, Methodist) on this chapter within the constraints. Below are verse‑by‑verse notes from what was found.

---

## Jeremiah 22 — Verse‑by‑Verse Notes

### v. 1
**“Go down to the palace of the king of Judah…”**

- **Gill** notes that “go down” reflects a literal descent from the temple mount to the palace, which sat on a lower eminence. The king addressed is Jehoiakim (then reigning), and this prophecy was delivered years before the events of chapter 21, though it is placed here to reinforce the warning.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Precept Austin** (citing the NET Bible note) says the same: the temple sat higher than the palace; “go down” is a geographical description. It also stresses that God’s word must be delivered directly into the seat of power, where resistance is greatest and where accountability is highest.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** adds that this continues the prophecy of chapter 21, directed to the house of David. The command “Go down” shows that Jeremiah must go directly to the king, not preach from a safe distance.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

---

### v. 2
**“Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David…”**

- **Gill** explains that invoking “the throne of David” was meant to remind the king of his illustrious ancestor and prompt him to follow David’s example. The summons includes the king’s servants (courtiers, nobles, privy counsellors) and all who enter the palace gates.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Precept Austin** (citing Wiersbe) notes a dual meaning of “house” throughout the chapter: both the physical palace and the Davidic dynasty. By invoking David’s throne, Jeremiah reminds the king that legitimacy depends on obedience to God’s covenant (2 Samuel 7:12–16).  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

---

### v. 3
**“Administer justice and righteousness. Rescue the victim of robbery… Do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow…”**

- **Guzik** says this command assumes there was great corruption and injustice at the highest levels of the kingdom. The king was called to perform his responsibilities in a godly and righteous way.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill** notes that the stranger, fatherless, and widow are those least able to defend themselves, and God has a peculiar regard for them. Kings and magistrates, as God’s deputies, are to protect such persons. Jehoiakim is guilty of the very crimes listed (see v. 17).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Precept Austin** expands: “justice” is how you treat others, “righteousness” is how you live before God. The vulnerable three groups (alien, orphan, widow) are the classic Deuteronomic triad (Deut. 10:18–19); how a people treats the weak measures their faithfulness to God. The command to “not shed innocent blood” condemns the ultimate injustice (cf. 2 Kings 21:16; 24:4).  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

- **Piper (Desiring God)** applies this broadly: if this is what kings were to do, how much more should believers under King Jesus move toward those with the greatest need.  
  https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-will-raise-up-for-david-a-righteous-branch

---

### v. 4
**“For if you will indeed carry out these commands, then kings who sit on David’s throne will enter through the gates…”**

- **Guzik**: repentance and justice would be rewarded; rejection would be punished. The choice was set before Judah and her rulers. He cites Kidner: there was still time for the house of David to “recover strongly.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: if the kings do their duty, there will never be a want of successors of David’s seed; a race of kings will sit on his throne in all after ages, entering the palace gates in royal pomp.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Precept Austin**: the “if…then” structure makes this a conditional promise. The image of kings “riding in chariots and on horses” symbolizes royal prosperity, stability, and divine favour. This echoes the conditional promise in Jeremiah 17:24–25.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

---

### v. 5
**“But if you do not obey these words, then I swear by Myself… that this house will become a pile of rubble.”**

- **Gill**: God swears by Himself because He can swear by no greater (Heb. 6:13). When God swears to a threatening, it shows the certainty and irreversibility of the judgment. “This house” means the king’s palace specifically.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Precept Austin** notes that “I swear by Myself” appears only here in the Bible in this exact wording (cf. Gen. 22:16; Amos 6:8). The oath conveys finality: no one, not even a king on David’s throne, is above God’s law.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

- **Matthew Henry**: sin will be the ruin of the houses of princes as well as of common men.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 6
**“You are like Gilead to Me, like the summit of Lebanon; but I will surely turn you into a desert…”**

- **Guzik**: Gilead and Lebanon were choice regions. God used these valued places to show how valued the house of David was to Him. Trapp adds: “High and happy, as those fruitful mountains, famous for spicery.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: the royal palace, for its wealth and stateliness (built with cedar), was like fertile Gilead and the top of Lebanon. Yet God would make it a wilderness. The language “if I do not make thee…” is an oath form showing certain accomplishment.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Precept Austin**: Gilead was known for rich pastures and healing balm (Jer. 8:22); Lebanon for majestic cedars. The imagery expresses both God’s affection and the severity of coming judgment upon the once‑precious royal house.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

---

### v. 7
**“I will appoint destroyers against you… they will cut down the choicest of your cedars and throw them into the fire.”**

- **Gill**: “I will prepare” is literally “I will consecrate” — the Babylonians are instruments of divine vengeance, set apart for this work. The “choice cedars” are the king’s sons, princes, and nobles, or the stately cedar‑lined buildings themselves that the Chaldeans would burn (Jer. 52:13).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Guzik**: God would not fight for Judah against Babylon; instead He would fight against them, preparing the soldiers Himself.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

---

### vv. 8–9
**“Many nations will pass by this city and ask… ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing?’ … ‘Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD… and worshiped other gods.’”**

- **Guzik**: the nations would see the destruction and wonder — was Israel’s God weaker than Babylon’s gods? The answer is simple: Judah forsook the covenant and turned to idolatry.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill** adds an interesting observation: this seems to refer not only to the first destruction by Nebuchadnezzar but also to the second by the Romans. After the Gospel spread among Gentiles, they had a better understanding of the true God and the real cause of the Jews’ ruin.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Matthew Henry**: God destroys neither persons, cities, nor nations except for sin; even in this world He often makes plain for what crimes punishment comes.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 10
**“Do not weep for the dead king; do not mourn his loss. Weep bitterly for the one who is exiled…”**

- **Gill**: “the dead” is Josiah, the godly king slain at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chron. 35:24). “Him that goeth away” is Jehoahaz (Shallum), deposed after three months and carried to Egypt. Josiah’s death, while tragic, was preferable to Shallum’s living exile, because Josiah was taken away from the evil to come.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Guzik** (citing Feinberg): “Jeremiah tells the nation at large that they need not mourn the death of the godly king Josiah.” The fate of Shallum in exile was worse than his father’s heroic death in battle.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Matthew Henry**: dying saints may be justly envied, while living sinners are justly pitied.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### vv. 11–12
**“Concerning Shallum son of Josiah… He will never return, but he will die in the place to which he was exiled…”**

- **Gill**: Shallum is Jehoahaz (confirmed by 1 Chron. 3:15). He reigned three months, was deposed by Pharaoh Necho, and died in Egypt. The prophecy was given in Jehoiakim’s reign while Shallum was still alive in captivity; it assures the people they should have no hope of his return.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Guzik** (citing Harrison): Jehoahaz succeeded Josiah in 609 BC, reigned three months, was taken to Riblah and then Egypt where he died.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Matthew Henry**: Shallum is “likely to live and die a wretched captive.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 13
**“Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness… who makes his countrymen serve without pay…”**

- **Gill**: this woe is directed at Jehoiakim. He built or enlarged his palace with money unjustly gotten and by not paying workmen — a crying sin in any person, much more in a king (cf. James 5:4).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Guzik** (citing Cundall): Jehoiakim faced a crippling tax imposed by Egypt (2 Kings 23:33ff.), extracted money from his subjects by heavy taxation, and then forced them to build his lavish palace without wages. Thompson adds a “democratic note”: the king is called the “neighbour” of his builder.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

---

### v. 14
**“I will build myself a great palace, with spacious upper rooms… panels it with cedar, and paints it with vermilion.”**

- **Gill** gives a lengthy note on the vermilion (Hebrew *shashar*): some render it “sinopis” (red ochre from Sinope), others “indicum” (indigo), and others “cinnabar” or vermilion. Whatever the precise pigment, the point is luxurious ornamentation at others’ expense.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Guzik** (citing Meyer): “Its width of space could not obliterate the memory of the forced and unpaid labour by which it had been reared. And God would plead and avenge the cause of those oppressed labourers.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

---

### v. 15
**“Does it make you a king to excel in cedar? Did not your father have food and drink? He administered justice and righteousness, and so it went well with him.”**

- **Guzik**: “Scathingly, Jeremiah asks Jehoiakim, ‘Does building palaces of cedar make you a king?’” Jehoiakim’s father Josiah lived modestly (“did eat and drink”) yet attended to the kingly duties of justice.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: the Targum paraphrases, “Dost thou think to be as the first king?” — meaning as great as David. True kingship is not proved by cedar panelling.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Matthew Henry**: Jehoiakim knew his father found the way of duty to be the way of comfort, yet would not tread in his steps.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 16
**“He took up the cause of the poor and needy… Is this not what it means to know Me?”**

- **Guzik**: this articulates a principle echoed in 1 John — our love and knowledge of God can be measured by how we treat other people. The rulers of Judah did not know God because they did not live out His love and justice.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Precept Austin**: knowing God is not intellectual alone; it is demonstrated in just, compassionate action toward the vulnerable. Josiah’s care for the poor was evidence that he truly knew the LORD.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

- **Piper (Desiring God)**: “Is not this what it means to know Me?” is God’s own definition. Josiah’s justice toward the poor and needy was the proof of his relationship with God.  
  https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-will-raise-up-for-david-a-righteous-branch

---

### v. 17
**“But your eyes and heart are set on nothing except your own dishonest gain, on shedding innocent blood, on practicing extortion and oppression.”**

- **Gill**: Jehoiakim’s fixation was covetousness, which led to the shedding of innocent blood and violent oppression. These were the very sins forbidden in v. 3.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Matthew Henry**: “Covetousness, which is the root of all evil, was at the bottom of all.” Jehoiakim made no conscience of shedding innocent blood.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### vv. 18–19
**“They will not mourn for him… He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.”**

- **Guzik** (citing Cundall): 2 Kings 24:6 gives no hint of this, but Jehoiakim’s death occurred while Jerusalem was besieged by Babylon. There is “plausible support” for a palace revolt in which the king was assassinated and his body thrown over the wall, signalling to the Babylonians that Jerusalem disassociated from his policy.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: no lamentation — no “Ah my brother” or “Ah his glory.” The burial of a donkey means no burial at all; his corpse was dragged out and left exposed.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Matthew Henry**: “He shall die unlamented, hateful for oppression and cruelty.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 20
**“Go up to Lebanon and cry out; raise your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers have been crushed.”**

- **Guzik**: the prophecy turns to Jerusalem personified. Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim represent distant places to which Judah looked for political alliances (her “lovers”). Spiritually, these were adulterous lovers, and now they were destroyed. Kidner adds that Abarim was the mountain range from which Moses viewed the Promised Land.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: “lovers” are the Egyptians and other allies in whom Judah trusted; now they are broken. The people are called to look from every high place and mourn.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 21
**“I warned you when you were secure. You said, ‘I will not listen.’ This has been your way from youth…”**

- **Guzik**: “This is one of the great weaknesses and tragedies of the human condition. In prosperity we often refuse to listen to God and He only has our attention in seasons of woe.” Kidner adds: “Happy if we can yet add the postscript from Psalm 119:67, ‘Before I was afflicted I went astray; but now I keep thy word.’”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Matthew Henry**: the Jewish state is described as “very haughty in a day of peace and safety.” Many never are ashamed of their sins until brought to the last extremity.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 22
**“The wind will drive away all your shepherds, and your lovers will go into captivity…”**

- **Guzik**: the “shepherds” (or “rulers” in some translations) and “lovers” (political allies) will both be swept away. Then Jerusalem will be ashamed and humiliated for all her wickedness.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: “the wind” likely represents the Chaldean army, which would consume the rulers and carry the allies into captivity.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 23
**“O inhabitant of Lebanon, nestled in the cedars, how you will groan when pangs of anguish come upon you…”**

- **Guzik** (citing Feinberg): “You who live in Lebanon” refers to the king and his nobles in their cedar palaces — they used so much cedar wood that they made their nest in the cedars. The labour‑pain simile depicts sudden, unavoidable anguish.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Precept Austin**: the image of a woman in labour is a frequent prophetic figure for inescapable judgment (cf. Jer. 4:31; 13:21; Isa. 13:8).  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-22-commentary

---

### v. 24
**“As surely as I live… even if you, Coniah son of Jehoiakim… were a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off.”**

- **Guzik**: perhaps Judah thought they were too loved by God to be judged. God says even if Coniah were as valued as the signet on His right hand, judgment would still come. Harrison: “Nothing can now prevent Jehoiachin’s exile, for in plucking off the signet God has rejected his leadership.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: “Coniah” is a shortened, perhaps contemptuous form of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin). A signet ring was highly valued and worn continually; yet God would cast him off.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Matthew Henry**: “Those that think themselves as signets on God’s right hand must not be secure, but fear lest they should be plucked thence.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 25
**“I will hand you over to those you dread… to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans.”**

- **Guzik**: God would (so to speak) take the signet ring off and give it to Nebuchadnezzar. Coniah would be handed over to the very people he feared most. This was precisely fulfilled — after a brief reign, Jehoiachin and other royals were taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:8–15).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: the ones Coniah dreaded were Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, who indeed took him captive.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### vv. 26–27
**“I will hurl you and the mother who gave you birth into another land… there you both will die. You will never return…”**

- **Gill**: the “mother” is likely the queen mother, who exercised considerable influence in the Judean court. Both would die in Babylon.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Guzik**: this was precisely fulfilled. Coniah and his family would long to return to the land but never would.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Matthew Henry**: “We know where we were born, but where we shall die we know not; it is enough that our God knows.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 28
**“Is this man Coniah a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants? Why are he and his descendants hurled out…?”**

- **Guzik** (citing Harrison): “a vessel in which is no pleasure” is the technical term for a pot of inferior grade — a sarcastic reference to the young Jehoiachin’s abilities. Trapp goes further: it is “by a modest periphrasis, a close‑stool [toilet], or piss‑pot (so Hosea 8:8).”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: the people had once delighted in Coniah, but now he is despised, a broken idol, a useless vessel.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 29
**“O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!”**

- **Guzik** (citing Feinberg): “The repetition implies strongest emphasis, solemnity, and intensity.” Kidner suggests that “earth” (KJV) is a better translation, giving the declaration universal scope, though the first hearers would take it as “O land.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: the triple address to the land of Israel emphasizes the importance and certainty of what follows.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

---

### v. 30
**“Enroll this man as childless… None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.”**

- **Guzik**: 1 Chronicles 3:17–18 lists Coniah’s sons; the command to “write him childless” means he should be *considered* as childless because his descendants are cursed. This curse — that no blood descendant of Jeconiah would ever sit on David’s throne — seems to threaten the Messianic promise (2 Samuel 7:16). The resolution: Matthew traces Jesus’ *legal* line through Joseph (including Jeconiah), while Luke traces Jesus’ *natural* line through Mary, who descended from David through Nathan, not Solomon. Thus Jesus inherits the legal right to the throne without being under the blood‑curse of Jeconiah.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/

- **Gill**: Solomon’s royal line ceased in Jeconiah. The curse “none of his seed shall prosper, sitting on the throne of David” was literally fulfilled; the royal line ended with him.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/22.htm

- **Matthew Henry**: “Whoever are childless, it is the Lord that writes them so; and those who take no care to do good in their days cannot expect to prosper.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/22.htm

---

## Tradition‑Specific Perspectives (What Was Found)

**Reformed / Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God):** In his sermon on Jeremiah 21:11–23:8, Piper treats chapter 22 as a “parade” of failed Davidic kings (Shallum, Jehoiakim, Coniah). Each failed to do justice and righteousness — the very thing God requires of those on David’s throne. The tension between the threat of annihilation and the promise of a lasting kingdom is resolved only in the “righteous Branch” of Jeremiah 23:5–6, whose name is “The LORD is our righteousness.” Piper stresses that this points to Jesus: “God alone can save or vindicate or justify his sinful people, and he will do it through this king.”  
https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-will-raise-up-for-david-a-righteous-branch

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik’s commentary, widely used in charismatic and evangelical circles, emphasizes the practical application of v. 16 — that knowing God is demonstrated by treating others justly. The resolution of the Coniah curse through the two genealogies of Jesus (Matthew and Luke) is a key apologetic point.  
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-22/
